CAPO: Counterfactual Credit Assignment in Sequential Cooperative Teams

Shripad Deshmukh ††thanks: Work done during a summer internship at Adobe Research, 2025. Affiliation: College of Information and Computer Sciences Affiliation: University of Massachusetts Amherst Email: svdeshmukh@cs.umass.edu    Jayakumar Subramanian Affiliation: Adobe Research Affiliation: San Jose, CA Email: jasubram@adobe.com    Raghavendra Addanki Affiliation: Adobe Research Affiliation: San Jose, CA Email: raddanki@adobe.com    Nikos Vlassis ††thanks: Corresponding author. Affiliation: Adobe Research Affiliation: San Jose, CA Email: vlassis@adobe.com
Abstract

In cooperative teams where agents act in a fixed order and share a single team reward, it is hard to know how much each agent contributed, and harder still when agents are updated one at a time because data collected earlier no longer reflects the new policies. We introduce the Sequential Aristocrat Utility (SeqAU), the unique per-agent learning signal that maximizes the individual learnability of each agent’s action, extending the classical framework of Wolpert and Tumer (2002) to this sequential setting. From SeqAU we derive CAPO (Counterfactual Advantage Policy Optimization), a critic-free policy-gradient algorithm. CAPO fits a per-agent reward decomposition from group rewards and computes the per-agent advantage in closed form plus a handful of forward passes through the current policy, requiring no extra environment calls beyond the initial batch. We give analytic bias and variance bounds and validate them on a controlled sequential bandit, where CAPO’s advantage over standard baselines grows with the team size. The framework is general; multi-LLM pipelines are a natural deployment target.

1 Introduction

Cooperative multi-agent systems arise in settings ranging from classical multi-agent reinforcement learning (Vlassis, 2007; Zhang et al., 2021) to modern pipelines composed of large language models and tool-using agents (Liu et al., 2025; Zhao et al., 2025; Chen et al., 2026). A common challenge in these systems is credit assignment: a team of agents receives only one team-level reward, and attributing this shared signal to individual agents is under-determined. Classical approaches handle this through centralized critics, whose input space grows exponentially in the team size (Foerster et al., 2018); through factored value functions, which introduce modeling constraints (Sunehag et al., 2018; Rashid et al., 2018; Wang et al., 2021; Peng et al., 2021); or through cumulative importance-sampling corrections, whose variance grows exponentially in the number of agents already updated (Kuba et al., 2022). The sequential cooperative setting, in which agents act in a fixed order and are updated one at a time within a batch, brings a further difficulty: updating an upstream agent shifts the distribution over downstream agents’ behavior, so rollouts collected under the pre-update policy are off-policy for subsequent updates within the same batch.

Contributions.

  • •

    Sequential Aristocrat Utility (Theorem 1). We extend the opacity-learnability framework of Wolpert and Tumer (2002) from simultaneous to sequential cooperative teams, and identify the unique prefix-dependent baseline that maximizes per-agent learnability; subtracting it from the team reward gives the Sequential Aristocrat Utility (SeqAU). This characterization and the upstream-cancellation identity (Appendix B) it implies are estimator-independent and apply to any sequential cooperative team.

  • •

    CAPO algorithm. We instantiate SeqAU as CAPO (Counterfactual Advantage Policy Optimization), a critic-free policy-gradient algorithm with three ingredients: an additive reward decomposition (Guestrin et al., 2002) fit by a least-squares ridge estimator, an upstream-cancellation identity that reduces the direct per-agent effect to a single-agent marginal, and fictitious sampling for the indirect effect (drawing counterfactual continuations from the current joint policy).

  • •

    Closed-form bias and variance analysis (Theorems 2–4). CAPO’s per-agent advantage bias is linear in the non-additivity residual; its variance adapts to inter-agent coupling (KK-independent in the factored-policy limit, O⁡(K−k)O(K-k) worst case), compared to the inherent Θ⁡(K)\Theta(K) of shared-baseline estimators like MA-GRPO (Liu et al., 2025) and O⁡(exp⁡K)O(\exp K) of cumulative-IS estimators like HAPPO (Kuba et al., 2022) and HA-GRPO; the policy-gradient MSE has no importance-sampling-ratio inflation. To our knowledge, such a closed-form bias-and-variance analysis of per-agent advantages is not available for decomposed-critic methods in the multi-agent literature.

  • •

    Empirical validation. On a controlled sequential-bandit testbed, per-agent advantage MSE scales as the theory predicts, CAPO’s end-to-end regret advantage over MA-GRPO, HA-GRPO, and C3 (Chen et al., 2026) grows with team size, and an ablation confirms the indirect-effect correction is necessary precisely when sequential-update non-stationarity is present.

We develop the framework in a contextual-bandit setting with sequential execution, where closed-form ground-truth advantages and exact variance calculations allow the theoretical claims to be tested cleanly. Extension to multi-agent language-model pipelines (Liu et al., 2025; Chen et al., 2026; Zhao et al., 2025), where sequential execution is native, is left to follow-up work.

2 Setup

We consider a cooperative team of KK agents acting in a contextual bandit (Lattimore and Szepesvári, 2020), each agent with action set of size AA. A context x∼𝒟x\sim\mathcal{D} is drawn, and the agents act in a fixed order 1,2,…,K1,2,\ldots,K. Each agent kk observes the prefix of upstream actions a<k=(a1,…,ak−1)a_{<k}=(a_{1},\ldots,a_{k-1}) and samples its own action ak∈𝒜ka_{k}\in\mathcal{A}_{k} from πk(⋅∣a<k,x;θk)\pi_{k}(\cdot\mid a_{<k},x;\theta_{k}). We write a=(a1,…,aK)a=(a_{1},\ldots,a_{K}) for the joint action and a>k=(ak+1,…,aK)a_{>k}=(a_{k+1},\ldots,a_{K}) for the suffix. The joint policy factorizes autoregressively, π⁡(a∣x)=∏kπk​(ak∣a<k,x)\pi(a\mid x)=\prod_{k}\pi_{k}(a_{k}\mid a_{<k},x), and we denote the induced downstream policy given a prefix-plus-focal action a≤ka_{\leq k} by π>k(⋅∣a≤k)=∏j>kπj(⋅∣a<j)\pi_{>k}(\cdot\mid a_{\leq k})=\prod_{j>k}\pi_{j}(\cdot\mid a_{<j}). The joint action produces a scalar team reward R⁡(a,x)∈[−Rmax,Rmax]R(a,x)\in[-R_{\max},R_{\max}] with conditional mean f(a,x)=𝔼[R∣a,x]f(a,x)=\mathbb{E}[R\mid a,x], and the team objective is V​(θ)=𝔼a∼πθ​[R]V(\theta)=\mathbb{E}_{a\sim\pi_{\theta}}[R]. For brevity we suppress xx throughout; every expression should be read pointwise in xx, and the theoretical results hold pointwise and therefore in expectation over 𝒟\mathcal{D}.

Execution order versus update order.

Two orderings recur throughout the paper. The execution order 1,2,…,K1,2,\ldots,K is fixed by the environment or task and determines which agents’ actions are visible to which, defining the prefix a<ka_{<k} and suffix a>ka_{>k} for each agent. The update order is the sequence in which agents’ policies are updated within a single outer training iteration. When updates are sequential, by the time it is agent kk’s turn to be updated the agents earlier in the update order have already moved from μ\mu to the new policy π\pi, so the data collected under μ\mu is now off-policy for agent kk, leading to a non-stationarity issue.

3 Opacity, Learnability, and the Sequential Aristocrat Utility

Following Wolpert and Tumer (2002), let the opacity of agent kk’s utility UkU_{k} at action aka_{k} be the variance of UkU_{k} over the randomness of all other agents’ actions, given aka_{k} and any information ℐ\mathcal{I} on which UkU_{k} is allowed to depend. Low opacity means that agent kk sees its own action’s effect on UkU_{k} without confounding from teammates’ choices; high opacity means the signal is drowned in teammate noise. A utility is factored with respect to the team reward if the argmax over agent kk’s actions of UkU_{k} coincides with the argmax of the team reward, holding all other agents fixed (Appendix A gives the formal definition). Factoredness ensures that optimizing UkU_{k} does not mislead the team; low opacity ensures that optimizing it is statistically tractable. For simultaneously-acting teams, Wolpert and Tumer (2002) showed that the Aristocrat Utility (AU),

UkAU​(a)=R⁡(a)−𝔼ak′∼πk​[R⁡(a−k,ak′)],U_{k}^{\mathrm{AU}}(a)\;=\;R(a)-\mathbb{E}_{a_{k}^{\prime}\sim\pi_{k}}[R(a_{-k},a_{k}^{\prime})],

is factored and has minimum opacity among all factored utilities whose baseline depends on a−ka_{-k} alone.

Sequential learnability.

In the sequential setting, agent kk’s information set naturally extends to include the upstream prefix a<ka_{<k}. We consider prefix-conditional utilities of the form Uk​(a)=R⁡(a)−bk​(a<k)U_{k}(a)=R(a)-b_{k}(a_{<k}), with baseline bkb_{k} any function of a<ka_{<k}, and define the suffix-averaged form of any utility UU,

U¯k(ak;a<k):=𝔼a>k∼π>k(⋅∣a≤k)[U(a)].\bar{U}_{k}(a_{k};a_{<k})\;:=\;\mathbb{E}_{a_{>k}\sim\pi_{>k}(\cdot\mid a_{\leq k})}[U(a)].

For a reference Markov kernel ρ(⋅∣a<k)∈Δ(𝒜k)\rho(\cdot\mid a_{<k})\in\Delta(\mathcal{A}_{k}) and moves ak1,ak2∈𝒜ka_{k}^{1},a_{k}^{2}\in\mathcal{A}_{k}, the sequential learnability of UkU_{k} is the signal-to-noise ratio

Λkseq​(Uk,ρ,ak1,ak2)=𝔼a<k​[U¯k​(ak1,a<k)−U¯k​(ak2,a<k)]𝔼a<k,ak∼ρ(⋅∣a<k)[Var(a<k,a>k)|ak[Uk]],\Lambda_{k}^{\mathrm{seq}}(U_{k};\rho,a_{k}^{1},a_{k}^{2})\;=\;\frac{\mathbb{E}_{a_{<k}}\!\bigl[\bar{U}_{k}(a_{k}^{1};a_{<k})-\bar{U}_{k}(a_{k}^{2};a_{<k})\bigr]}{\sqrt{\mathbb{E}_{a_{<k},\,a_{k}\sim\rho(\cdot\mid a_{<k})}\!\bigl[\mathrm{Var}_{(a_{<k},a_{>k})\mid a_{k}}[U_{k}]\bigr]}}, (1)

whose numerator measures how much the suffix-averaged utility shifts with the focal action, averaged over prefixes, and whose denominator measures how much UkU_{k} fluctuates under teammate behavior for a fixed focal action; both expectations and the inner variance are pointwise in a<ka_{<k}. The reference kernel is a degree of freedom; the natural choice, used throughout, is ρ(⋅∣a<k)=πk(⋅∣a<k)\rho(\cdot\mid a_{<k})=\pi_{k}(\cdot\mid a_{<k}).

Theorem 1 (Sequential Aristocrat Utility).

Within the class of sequential difference utilities {R−D(a<k):D:∏j<k𝒜j→ℝ}\{R-D(a_{<k}):D:\prod_{j<k}\mathcal{A}_{j}\to\mathbb{R}\}, all of which are factored with respect to RR, the sequential learnability Λkseq\Lambda_{k}^{\mathrm{seq}} is maximized for every prefix a<ka_{<k} and every pair (ak1,ak2)(a_{k}^{1},a_{k}^{2}), uniquely, by the baseline

D∗(a<k)=𝔼ak′∼ρ(⋅∣a<k),a>k′∼π>k(⋅∣a<k,ak′)[R(ak′,a<k,a>k′)].D^{*}(a_{<k})\;=\;\mathbb{E}_{a_{k}^{\prime}\sim\rho(\cdot\mid a_{<k}),\;a_{>k}^{\prime}\sim\pi_{>k}(\cdot\mid a_{<k},a_{k}^{\prime})}\!\bigl[R(a_{k}^{\prime},a_{<k},a_{>k}^{\prime})\bigr]. (2)

The resulting Sequential Aristocrat Utility is gkSeqAU​(a)=R⁡(a)−D∗​(a<k)g_{k}^{\mathrm{SeqAU}}(a)=R(a)-D^{*}(a_{<k}). Factoredness of the search class, uniqueness, and the full proof are in Appendix A.

Counterfactual advantage.

Setting ρ(⋅∣a<k)=πk(⋅∣a<k)\rho(\cdot\mid a_{<k})=\pi_{k}(\cdot\mid a_{<k}) in (2) gives the SeqAU-induced counterfactual advantage

AkSeqAU​(a≤k)=𝔼π​[R∣a≤k]−𝔼π​[R∣a<k],A_{k}^{\mathrm{SeqAU}}(a_{\leq k})\;=\;\mathbb{E}_{\pi}[R\mid a_{\leq k}]\;-\;\mathbb{E}_{\pi}[R\mid a_{<k}], (3)

the quantity that COMA (Foerster et al., 2018) estimates via a learned centralized critic in the simultaneous-action setting. The main contribution of this section is Theorem 1, which establishes that the baseline subtracted in (3), 𝔼π​[R∣a<k]\mathbb{E}_{\pi}[R\mid a_{<k}], is not merely a natural choice in the sequential setting but the unique learnability-maximizing one among prefix-conditional baselines, with no structural assumption on the team reward. Section 4 turns (3) into a tractable estimator via an additive decomposition of RR and an upstream-cancellation identity, recovering a direct/indirect form that collapses to Wolpert-Tumer’s Aristocrat Utility in the factored-policy limit.

4 CAPO: Counterfactual Advantage Policy Optimization

4.1 The estimation problem and three failure modes

Within an outer iteration, write π(0)=μ\pi^{(0)}=\mu for the rollout-collection joint policy and, for k≥1k\geq 1, π(k)\pi^{(k)} for the joint policy after agent kk has been updated; the joint policy at the moment of agent kk’s update is therefore π(k−1)\pi^{(k-1)}, which we call the current joint policy for that update. The SeqAU target (3) requires two conditional expectations of the team reward under π(k−1)\pi^{(k-1)}, neither directly available. Under sequential updates, π(k−1)\pi^{(k-1)} differs from μ\mu by exactly the upstream agents that have already moved, so the μ\mu-rollouts in the batch are not a direct match for either expectation. Estimating the SeqAU advantage therefore requires a structured reward-attribution estimator; three lines of prior work attempt this, and each fails in a specific way that motivates one ingredient of CAPO.

Centralized critic (COMA, DOP).

COMA (Foerster et al., 2018) learns 𝔼π​[R∣a]\mathbb{E}_{\pi}[R\mid a] as a centralized QQ-critic on the joint action and marginalizes the focal action at O⁡(|𝒜|K)O(|\mathcal{A}|^{K}) cost; DOP (Wang et al., 2021) reduces this via an additively factored critic. Both target simultaneous execution and do not address sequential-update drift.

Cumulative importance sampling (HA-GRPO).

HA-GRPO (Kuba et al., 2022) reweights the shared trajectory advantage by the cumulative prefix ∏j<kπj(j)/μj\prod_{j<k}\pi_{j}^{(j)}/\mu_{j}, whose variance grows exponentially in the number of agents already updated.

Replay-based counterfactual (C3).

C3 (Chen et al., 2026) replays the downstream pipeline at alternative focal actions under actual environment dynamics, paying one reward evaluation per replay. It assumes nothing about the reward structure but cannot scale when reward evaluation is expensive.

The three CAPO moves answer these in turn: an additive reward decomposition that makes per-agent attribution closed-form (Section 4.2), an upstream-cancellation identity that simplifies the SeqAU target to two cheap pieces (Section 4.3), and fictitious sampling that estimates the indirect effect under the current joint policy π(k−1)\pi^{(k-1)} without importance weights or replay (Section 4.4).

4.2 Additive reward model for closed-form per-agent attribution

The first failure mode (centralized-critic blowup) suggests trading generality for tractability. Following a long line of work on additive or factored team-reward decompositions in cooperative multi-agent RL (Guestrin et al., 2002; Kok and Vlassis, 2006; Sunehag et al., 2018; Wang et al., 2021), we model the expected team reward as

f⁡(a)=𝔼⁡[R∣a]=∑k=1Kφk​(ak).f(a)\;=\;\mathbb{E}[R\mid a]\;=\;\sum_{k=1}^{K}\varphi_{k}(a_{k}). (4)

This structure allows per-agent attribution to be recovered in closed form from a single linear regression rather than a learned critic. (Section 5 bounds the advantage bias incurred when the assumption is violated.) We estimate the per-agent components by regressing the team reward onto agent-action indicator features. Each joint action is encoded as ψ⁡(a)∈{0,1}d\psi(a)\in\{0,1\}^{d} with d=K​Ad=KA, the concatenation of per-agent one-hot vectors. Stacking the NN rollouts of a batch into a feature matrix Ψ∈ℝN×d\Psi\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times d} with reward vector r∈ℝNr\in\mathbb{R}^{N}, the ridge-regression estimator

φ^=(λ​I+Ψ⊤​Ψ)−1​Ψ⊤​r\hat{\varphi}\;=\;\bigl(\lambda I+\Psi^{\top}\Psi\bigr)^{-1}\Psi^{\top}r (5)

returns per-agent components whose concatenation φ^=(φ^1,…,φ^K)∈ℝd\hat{\varphi}=(\hat{\varphi}_{1},\ldots,\hat{\varphi}_{K})\in\mathbb{R}^{d} identifies the best additive approximation to ff under μ\mu. The solve is O⁡(d3)O(d^{3}), requires no gradient steps, and reuses the same NN rollouts the policy-gradient update would consume anyway. (At λ=0\lambda=0, this reduces to the slate pseudoinverse (Swaminathan et al., 2017), which targets the same additive linear structure for slate off-policy evaluation; we add the ridge regularizer to supply coverage where some per-agent actions are rare under μ\mu.) Per-coordinate variance of φ^\hat{\varphi} is bounded independently of KK (Theorem 3), which is what makes per-agent attribution cheap for arbitrarily large teams.

4.3 Upstream cancellation: focal advantage reduces to direct + indirect

Plugging the additive approximation f^​(a)=∑kφ^k​(ak)\hat{f}(a)=\sum_{k}\hat{\varphi}_{k}(a_{k}) into the SeqAU advantage (3) produces a sum over all KK agents in both conditional expectations 𝔼π(k−1)​[f^∣a≤k]\mathbb{E}_{\pi^{(k-1)}}[\hat{f}\mid a_{\leq k}] and 𝔼π(k−1)​[f^∣a<k]\mathbb{E}_{\pi^{(k-1)}}[\hat{f}\mid a_{<k}]. Under the autoregressive factorization of π(k−1)\pi^{(k-1)}, contributions from agents upstream of kk depend only on the prefix a<ka_{<k} and appear identically in both terms; they cancel exactly in the difference and need not be estimated. What remains is a clean two-piece advantage:

A^kLS(a≤k)=φ^k(ak)−𝔼ak′∼πk(⋅∣a<k)[φ^k(ak′)]⏟Dk:direct effect (closed form)+∑j>k(𝔼π>k|a≤k​[φ^j]−𝔼π>k|a<k​[φ^j])⏟Ik:indirect effect.\hat{A}_{k}^{\mathrm{LS}}(a_{\leq k})\;=\;\underbrace{\hat{\varphi}_{k}(a_{k})-\mathbb{E}_{a_{k}^{\prime}\sim\pi_{k}(\cdot\mid a_{<k})}[\hat{\varphi}_{k}(a_{k}^{\prime})]}_{D_{k}:\text{direct effect (closed form)}}\;+\;\underbrace{\sum_{j>k}\!\bigl(\mathbb{E}_{\pi_{>k}\mid a_{\leq k}}[\hat{\varphi}_{j}]-\mathbb{E}_{\pi_{>k}\mid a_{<k}}[\hat{\varphi}_{j}]\bigr)}_{I_{k}:\text{indirect effect}}. (6)

Direct effect.

DkD_{k} depends only on φ^k\hat{\varphi}_{k} and the current marginal πk(⋅∣a<k)\pi_{k}(\cdot\mid a_{<k}) and is closed-form. In the factored-policy limit where IkI_{k} vanishes, DkD_{k} alone is the per-agent advantage that DOP (Wang et al., 2021) obtains in the simultaneous-execution setting via critic-side cancellation, attained here reward-side.

Indirect effect.

IkI_{k} captures how agent kk’s action shifts the conditional distribution over downstream agents’ actions, and through them the reward contributions φ^j\hat{\varphi}_{j} for j>kj>k. This term is the new content of the sequential setting; estimating it is the subject of Section 4.4. The full algebraic derivation of (6) is in Appendix B.

4.4 Fictitious sampling for the indirect effect

The indirect-effect expectations in (6) require conditional distributions over downstream actions under π(k−1)\pi^{(k-1)}, which the μ\mu-rollouts cannot supply. CAPO addresses this by drawing fictitious continuations from π(k−1)\pi^{(k-1)} conditioned on each rollout’s μ\mu-realized prefix, rather than reweighting the μ\mu-rollouts (the HA-GRPO approach, with exponential IS-variance cost) or re-executing the downstream pipeline in the real environment (the C3 approach, with one reward evaluation per replay). For each rollout nn, we generate two sample sets:

a~>k(n,ℓ)∼π>k(k−1)(⋅|a≤k(n)),ℓ=1,…,L,\tilde{a}_{>k}^{(n,\ell)}\;\sim\;\pi_{>k}^{(k-1)}\!\bigl(\cdot\,\big|\,a_{\leq k}^{(n)}\bigr),\qquad\ell=1,\ldots,L, (7)
(a~k(n,ℓ),a~>k′(n,ℓ))∼πk(k−1)(⋅|a<k(n))⋅π>k(k−1)(⋅|a<k(n),a~k(n,ℓ)),ℓ=1,…,L,\bigl(\tilde{a}_{k}^{(n,\ell)},\tilde{a}_{>k}^{\prime(n,\ell)}\bigr)\;\sim\;\pi_{k}^{(k-1)}\!\bigl(\cdot\,\big|\,a_{<k}^{(n)}\bigr)\cdot\pi_{>k}^{(k-1)}\!\bigl(\cdot\,\big|\,a_{<k}^{(n)},\tilde{a}_{k}^{(n,\ell)}\bigr),\qquad\ell=1,\ldots,L, (8)

and form the per-rollout Monte Carlo estimate of the SeqAU advantage:

A^k(n)=1L​∑ℓ=1L[f^​(a≤k(n),a~>k(n,ℓ))−f^​(a<k(n),a~k(n,ℓ),a~>k′(n,ℓ))].\hat{A}_{k}^{(n)}\;=\;\frac{1}{L}\sum_{\ell=1}^{L}\Bigl[\hat{f}\bigl(a_{\leq k}^{(n)},\tilde{a}_{>k}^{(n,\ell)}\bigr)\;-\;\hat{f}\bigl(a_{<k}^{(n)},\tilde{a}_{k}^{(n,\ell)},\tilde{a}_{>k}^{\prime(n,\ell)}\bigr)\Bigr]. (9)

The first term holds the prefix-plus-focal-action at its realized value and averages over downstream completions drawn from π>k(k−1)(⋅∣a≤k(n))\pi_{>k}^{(k-1)}(\cdot\mid a_{\leq k}^{(n)}); the second integrates the focal action out under πk(k−1)(⋅∣a<k(n))\pi_{k}^{(k-1)}(\cdot\mid a_{<k}^{(n)}) and then draws downstream completions from π>k(k−1)(⋅∣a<k(n),a~k(n,ℓ))\pi_{>k}^{(k-1)}(\cdot\mid a_{<k}^{(n)},\tilde{a}_{k}^{(n,\ell)}). Their difference is exactly Dk+IkD_{k}+I_{k} from (6), with the direct effect computed in closed form and the indirect effect estimated by the fictitious draws. The draws require only policy forward passes, not reward evaluations or environment interactions; evaluating f^\hat{f} is a table lookup of dimension KK.

The fictitious estimator avoids both pathologies. It does not reweight, so no IS variance accumulates with kk; the effective sample size is LL for every agent, independent of position within the team. It does not replay, so no reward evaluations are spent beyond the initial batch. The cost asymmetry against C3 is structural in regimes where reward evaluation dominates (external verifiers, code executors, graders, human raters); the cost asymmetry against HA-GRPO is statistical, with no exponential-in-kk variance entering the gradient (Theorem 4).

We note that the prefixes a<k(n)a_{<k}^{(n)} and a≤k(n)a_{\leq k}^{(n)} in (9) are those realized under the rollout-collection policy μ\mu; only the downstream continuation (and the counterfactual focal action in (8)) are drawn from π(k−1)\pi^{(k-1)}. The outer average over nn therefore integrates the advantage against the μ\mu-prefix distribution rather than the π<k(k−1)\pi_{<k}^{(k-1)}-prefix distribution. Under sequential updates this introduces a prefix-drift bias already captured by Theorem 2 through the per-agent total-variation drift δ¯=maxj⁡‖πj−μj‖1\bar{\delta}=\max_{j}\|\pi_{j}-\mu_{j}\|_{1}; we accept it in exchange for avoiding a cumulative importance-sampling prefix.

4.5 Algorithm and per-iteration cost

Algorithm 1 collects the three CAPO moves into a single outer iteration. CAPO performs (i) one ridge solve on the batch (Section 4.2, O⁡(d3)O(d^{3})), (ii) 2​N​K​L2NKL fictitious continuations across all agents and rollouts (Section 4.4, policy inference only), and (iii) K⋅MK\cdot M inner PPO updates on the per-agent advantages (Section 4.3). The real-rollout count matches the GRPO baseline (both methods collect NN trajectories per iteration); the additional cost is the ridge solve and the policy-only fictitious draws, neither of which scales with the cost of the reward signal.

5 Theoretical Properties

We characterize the statistical properties of the CAPO advantage estimator (6). Let ε​(a)=f^​(a)−f​(a)\varepsilon(a)=\hat{f}(a)-f(a) denote the residual of the additive approximation, so that ‖ε‖∞\|\varepsilon\|_{\infty} measures the worst-case non-additivity. Let Gμ=𝔼μ​[ψ⁡(a)​ψ​(a)⊤]∈ℝd×dG_{\mu}=\mathbb{E}_{\mu}[\psi(a)\psi(a)^{\top}]\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times d} be the population Gram matrix of the indicator features with smallest eigenvalue κμ=λmin​(Gμ)\kappa_{\mu}=\lambda_{\min}(G_{\mu}). We assume κμ>0\kappa_{\mu}>0, that is, every per-agent action has positive probability under the marginal of μ\mu; the ridge regularizer λ>0\lambda>0 supplies the coverage otherwise. All rewards are bounded, |R⁡(a)|≤Rmax|R(a)|\leq R_{\max}. Proofs are given in Appendix C.

Advantage bias under non-additive rewards.

Theorem 2 (Advantage bias).

Let Δk=A^kLS−AkSeqAU\Delta_{k}=\hat{A}_{k}^{\mathrm{LS}}-A_{k}^{\mathrm{SeqAU}} denote the CAPO advantage bias, where A^kLS\hat{A}_{k}^{\mathrm{LS}} is computed from φ^\hat{\varphi} fit on μ\mu-rollouts. For any joint action (a<k,ak)(a_{<k},a_{k}),

|Δk(a≤k)|≤𝔼π≥k|a<k[δkε(a−k)]+∥ε∥∞⋅maxak,ak′∥π>k(⋅∣a<k,ak)−π>k(⋅∣a<k,ak′)∥1,|\Delta_{k}(a_{\leq k})|\;\leq\;\mathbb{E}_{\pi_{\geq k}\mid a_{<k}}[\delta_{k}^{\varepsilon}(a_{-k})]\;+\;\|\varepsilon\|_{\infty}\cdot\max_{a_{k},a_{k}^{\prime}}\!\bigl\|\pi_{>k}(\cdot\mid a_{<k},a_{k})-\pi_{>k}(\cdot\mid a_{<k},a_{k}^{\prime})\bigr\|_{1},

where δkε​(a−k)=maxak,ak′⁡|ε⁡(a<k,ak,a>k)−ε⁡(a<k,ak′,a>k)|\delta_{k}^{\varepsilon}(a_{-k})=\max_{a_{k},a_{k}^{\prime}}|\varepsilon(a_{<k},a_{k},a_{>k})-\varepsilon(a_{<k},a_{k}^{\prime},a_{>k})|. If both target and logging policies factor across agents, π⁡(a)=∏kπk​(ak)\pi(a)=\prod_{k}\pi_{k}(a_{k}) and μ⁡(a)=∏kμk​(ak)\mu(a)=\prod_{k}\mu_{k}(a_{k}), the bound specializes to

|Δk​(ak)|≤ 2​(K−1)​δ¯​‖ε‖∞,δ¯=maxj⁡‖πj−μj‖1,|\Delta_{k}(a_{k})|\;\leq\;2(K-1)\,\bar{\delta}\,\|\varepsilon\|_{\infty},\qquad\bar{\delta}=\max_{j}\|\pi_{j}-\mu_{j}\|_{1},

the maximum per-agent total-variation drift between target and logging policies.

Bias has two channels. The first vanishes when the additive residual is insensitive to the focal action; the second vanishes when the joint policy is factored and downstream agents do not see the focal action. In a GRPO loop with μ(t)=π(t−1)\mu^{(t)}=\pi^{(t-1)} and inner-PPO drift δ¯=O⁡(M​η)\bar{\delta}=O(M\eta), the per-batch bias under factored policies is O⁡(K​M​η​‖ε‖∞)O(KM\eta\|\varepsilon\|_{\infty}), small whenever the inner step size is moderate or the reward is close to additive. The λint\lambda_{\mathrm{int}}-sweep of Section 6.2 tests this bound directly.

Advantage variance under additive rewards.

Theorem 3 (Ridge-attribution variance).

Suppose ff is additive, and condition on exact evaluation of the indirect-effect expectations in (6) (i.e., the L→∞L\to\infty limit of the fictitious-sampling estimator). Replacing the sample Gram matrix Ψ⊤​Ψ\Psi^{\top}\Psi by its population version N​GμNG_{\mu},11 1 The sample-Gram fluctuations around N​GμNG_{\mu} contribute an O⁡(1/N)O(1/\sqrt{N}) correction that does not affect the KK-scaling statement. the variance of the direct-effect component DkD_{k} of the CAPO advantage at any agent kk and any focal action aka_{k} satisfies

Var⁡(Dk​(a≤k))≤2​Rmax2λ+N​κμ,\mathrm{Var}\!\bigl(D_{k}(a_{\leq k})\bigr)\;\leq\;\frac{2\,R_{\max}^{2}}{\lambda+N\,\kappa_{\mu}},

independent of KK, the feature dimension dd, and the interaction structure of ff. The full advantage A^kLS=Dk+Ik\hat{A}_{k}^{\mathrm{LS}}=D_{k}+I_{k} adds at most 2​(K−k)2(K-k) to the ℓ2\ell_{2}-coefficient norm of the underlying linear functional of φ^\hat{\varphi}, giving a worst-case bound of (2+2​(K−k))​Rmax2λ+N​κμ\frac{(2+2(K-k))\,R_{\max}^{2}}{\lambda+N\,\kappa_{\mu}}. In the factored-policy limit, Ik≡0I_{k}\equiv 0 and the KK-independent direct-effect bound applies to the full advantage exactly.

Remark 1.

At finite LL, the full CAPO advantage carries an additional O⁡(1/L)O(1/L) Monte Carlo variance from the indirect-effect estimator, whose dependence on KK inherits the scaling of f^\hat{f} (in the worst case O⁡(K)O(K), when f^\hat{f} is a sum of KK bounded per-agent contributions).

Two comparisons are immediate. The shared-baseline advantage A^kMA=R−R¯\hat{A}^{\mathrm{MA}}_{k}=R-\bar{R} used by MA-GRPO (Liu et al., 2025) has variance O⁡(K​σφ2/N)O(K\sigma_{\varphi}^{2}/N) when the per-agent reward contributions are independent; this scaling is inherent, not worst-case, because the team reward itself has KK-way variance. The importance-sampled prefix advantage used by HAPPO (Kuba et al., 2022) and HA-GRPO has variance O⁡(∏j<k𝔼μ​[Yj2]⋅Rmax2/N)O(\prod_{j<k}\mathbb{E}_{\mu}[Y_{j}^{2}]\cdot R_{\max}^{2}/N), exponential in the number of agents already updated whenever the per-agent importance ratios have second moment greater than one. CAPO’s variance, by contrast, adapts to the coupling structure: KK-independent in the factored-policy limit and at most O⁡(K−k)O(K-k) in the worst case, matching the shared-baseline KK-scaling only when downstream agents are maximally sensitive to upstream actions and collapsing to KK-independent whenever they are not (Section 6.1 confirms this empirically).

Gradient mean-squared error.

Theorem 4 (Gradient MSE).

Let gk∗=𝔼π(k−1)​[Ak​sk]g_{k}^{*}=\mathbb{E}_{\pi^{(k-1)}}[A_{k}s_{k}] be the true policy gradient under the joint policy at the moment of agent kk’s update, with sk=∇θk​log​πk​(ak∣a<k)s_{k}=\nabla_{\theta_{k}}\log\pi_{k}(a_{k}\mid a_{<k}), and let BkB_{k} be a uniform bound on |Δk||\Delta_{k}| from Theorem 2. Consider the idealized on-policy estimator g^k=L−1​∑ℓA^kLS,(ℓ)​sk(ℓ)\hat{g}_{k}=L^{-1}\sum_{\ell}\hat{A}_{k}^{\mathrm{LS},(\ell)}s_{k}^{(\ell)} formed from LL rollouts drawn from π(k−1)\pi^{(k-1)} (the practical CAPO gradient averages per-rollout advantages over μ\mu-rollouts with fictitious continuations, eq. (9); its exact finite-sample analysis is left to future work). This estimator satisfies

𝔼​‖g^k−gk∗‖2≤2L​Varπ(k−1)​(Ak​sk)+ 2​Bk2​𝔼π(k−1)​[‖sk‖2].\mathbb{E}\|\hat{g}_{k}-g_{k}^{*}\|^{2}\;\leq\;\frac{2}{L}\mathrm{Var}_{\pi^{(k-1)}}(A_{k}s_{k})\;+\;2B_{k}^{2}\,\mathbb{E}_{\pi^{(k-1)}}[\|s_{k}\|^{2}].

The first term is the standard on-policy REINFORCE variance without importance-sampling-ratio inflation, because the fictitious rollouts are drawn directly from π(k−1)\pi^{(k-1)} rather than reweighted from μ\mu. The second term is the bias contribution, bounded by Theorem 2. Sequential-update HA-GRPO pays for the same drift via a cumulative IS prefix whose variance is exponential in kk; CAPO pays via additive-residual bias that is linear in ‖ε‖∞\|\varepsilon\|_{\infty} and zero when the reward is strictly additive.

6 Experiments

We validate the theoretical claims of Sections 3–5 on a controlled sequential cooperative-bandit testbed admitting closed-form ground-truth advantages. The setup allows us to measure advantage-estimation quality directly as well as end-to-end optimization performance. We report four experiments: per-agent advantage MSE as a function of team size (Section 6.1); robustness of the advantage estimator to violations of the additivity assumption (Section 6.2); end-to-end policy optimization under sequential-update non-stationarity (Section 6.3); and an ablation testing whether the indirect-effect correction is doing work (Section 6.4).

Common setup.

Agents have action sets of size A=4A=4; team rewards are f⁡(a)=∑kφk​(ak)+λint​∑k<ℓgk​ℓ​(ak,aℓ)f(a)=\sum_{k}\varphi_{k}(a_{k})+\lambda_{\mathrm{int}}\sum_{k<\ell}g_{k\ell}(a_{k},a_{\ell}) with φk\varphi_{k} and gk​ℓg_{k\ell} drawn per seed with matched variance so that λint=1\lambda_{\mathrm{int}}=1 makes the pairwise variance equal to the additive variance. Advantage ground truth is computed by exact marginalization. Policies condition only on the immediately preceding action, πk(⋅∣ak−1)\pi_{k}(\cdot\mid a_{k-1}), and a non-stationarity parameter ρ≥0\rho\geq 0 concentrates the initial conditional distributions toward their upstream condition (Appendix E); ρ=0\rho=0 gives near-uniform initial policies and larger ρ\rho gives increasingly concentrated ones. We compare CAPO against three baselines defined in Section 2: MA-GRPO, HA-GRPO, and C3. The MSE experiments in Sections 6.1–6.2 use the closed-form ridge estimator of (5) and test Theorem 3’s bounds directly. The optimization experiments in Sections 6.3–6.4 use a related fictitious-sampling estimator of φ^\hat{\varphi} that shares the same population target as the ridge solve; finite-sample analysis of this practical variant is left to future work.

6.1 Per-agent advantage estimation quality

We measure the mean-squared error between estimated and ground-truth per-agent advantages, as a function of the team size KK with λint=0\lambda_{\mathrm{int}}=0 (additive reward) and N=16N=16 rollouts per batch. Figure 2 reports the advantage MSE averaged over agents and 30 seeds. CAPO’s MSE is roughly flat in KK, consistent with the direct-effect bound of Theorem 3; in this testbed the indirect-effect contribution to the MSE is small relative to the ridge-attribution variance, so the KK-independent direct-effect scaling carries over to the full advantage empirically. The shared-baseline MA-GRPO grows linearly in KK, consistent with the O⁡(K)O(K) scaling of shared advantages; HA-GRPO grows faster than linear because the prefix importance ratio amplifies noise at downstream agents; C3 tracks CAPO’s shape but with a consistent offset attributable to prefix-filtering variance. The per-agent breakdown at K=16K=16 (Appendix D) shows that CAPO’s MSE is essentially flat across agent positions, while HA-GRPO grows with agent index as the IS prefix accumulates. At K=16K=16, CAPO’s average MSE is roughly 2×2\times smaller than C3’s, 30×30\times smaller than MA-GRPO’s, and 46×46\times smaller than HA-GRPO’s. For the shared-baseline methods (MA-GRPO, HA-GRPO), which emit a single trajectory advantage shared across agents, the per-agent estimate is the shared scalar evaluated at each rollout’s prefix and focal action; the MSE is computed against the same per-agent ground truth as for CAPO and C3.

6.2 Robustness to non-additive rewards

Theorem 2 bounds the CAPO advantage bias linearly in the additive residual ‖ε‖∞\|\varepsilon\|_{\infty}. We probe this prediction by sweeping λint∈{0,0.25,0.5,0.75,1.0}\lambda_{\mathrm{int}}\in\{0,0.25,0.5,0.75,1.0\} at K=4K=4, with all other parameters fixed. Figure 2 reports the MSE. CAPO’s MSE grows monotonically with λint\lambda_{\mathrm{int}}, from 0.030.03 at λint=0\lambda_{\mathrm{int}}=0 to 0.920.92 at λint=1\lambda_{\mathrm{int}}=1, consistent with the predicted linear-in-‖ε‖∞\|\varepsilon\|_{\infty} scaling. C3 is nearly flat across the sweep, reflecting that it does not assume additivity. The shared-baseline methods scale roughly linearly with λint\lambda_{\mathrm{int}}, tracking the growth of the reward magnitude. CAPO remains the best of the four methods across the full range, including at λint=1\lambda_{\mathrm{int}}=1 where half of the reward variance is from pairwise interactions.

6.3 End-to-end policy optimization

We now evaluate end-to-end policy optimization. The sweep covers K∈{2,4,6,8,10}K\in\{2,4,6,8,10\}, λint∈{0,0.25,0.5,0.75,1.0}\lambda_{\mathrm{int}}\in\{0,0.25,0.5,0.75,1.0\}, and initial-policy concentration ρ∈{0,1,2}\rho\in\{0,1,2\}, with all four methods consuming the same total real-environment-interaction budget (per-iteration counts therefore differ between methods; C3 runs 25 iterations across all KK to absorb its per-iteration replay cost, while CAPO, MA-GRPO, and HA-GRPO run 25​(K+2)25(K+2) iterations). 300 seeds per cell. Per-(K,λint,ρ)(K,\lambda_{\mathrm{int}},\rho) AUC and regret trajectories are in Appendix F.

Table 1 summarizes mean regret AUC per (K,method)(K,\text{method}), averaged over λint\lambda_{\mathrm{int}} and ρ\rho (lower is better). Three patterns emerge, all matching the theory of Section 5.

At K=2K=2, MA-GRPO suffices.

With only two agents and one upstream-update per batch, the shared trajectory advantage is a perfectly adequate learning signal; MA-GRPO has the lowest AUC and HA-GRPO’s IS prefix (a single-term correction here) is competitive. CAPO’s per-agent counterfactual machinery is not wrong, but the extra Monte Carlo variance costs a bit without a proportionate gain. When the team is small, simpler is better.

CAPO crosses over around K=4K=4 and pulls ahead with KK.

For K≥6K\geq 6, CAPO has the lowest AUC across all cells, with the gap over MA-GRPO widening from ≈0.01\approx 0.01 at K=4K=4 to ≈0.02\approx 0.02 at K=10K=10. This matches the Θ⁡(K)\Theta(K) inherent variance of the shared-baseline advantage (the team reward itself has KK-way variance, and no amount of centering escapes it), while CAPO’s variance adapts to the coupling structure and does not grow as starkly.

HA-GRPO degrades rapidly with KK.

The cumulative IS prefix’s variance is exponential in the number of agents already updated; by K=10K=10, HA-GRPO approaches C3 in AUC, despite starting comparable to MA-GRPO at K=2K=2. C3 itself consistently trails all other methods: under matched real-env budget, its O⁡(K2)O(K^{2}) per-iteration replay cost forces only 25 iterations, leaving little room for the policy to improve.

6.4 Ablation: is the indirect effect doing work?

Section 4 decomposes the CAPO advantage into a closed-form direct effect and a fictitious-sample indirect effect. The indirect effect is the non-trivial piece and requires the fictitious-sampling machinery. To test whether it is doing work, we compare CAPO against CAPO-Direct, an ablation that retains the closed-form direct-effect exp-update but drops the indirect effect. CAPO-Direct is not a straw-man construction: in the simultaneous-execution limit where the joint policy factorizes, the indirect effect vanishes identically and SeqAU reduces to Wolpert-Tumer’s AU applied pointwise at each prefix. CAPO-Direct computes exactly this per-prefix AU, which is also the single-agent target that DOP (Wang et al., 2021) obtains in the simultaneous-execution setting via critic-side cancellation. Figure 3 sweeps ρ∈{0,5,10,20}\rho\in\{0,5,10,20\} across K∈{2,4,8}K\in\{2,4,8\} and λint∈{0,0.25,0.5,0.75,1.0}\lambda_{\mathrm{int}}\in\{0,0.25,0.5,0.75,1.0\} (regret trajectories per λint\lambda_{\mathrm{int}} in Appendix G). At ρ=0\rho=0 the downstream coupling vanishes and CAPO-Direct matches or slightly outperforms CAPO, consistent with the factored-policy limit of Theorem 1: the indirect-effect Monte Carlo adds variance without signal when there is no signal to capture. As ρ\rho grows the indirect effect becomes the dominant part of the per-agent advantage; CAPO pulls ahead cleanly by ρ=10\rho=10 and the gap widens further at ρ=20\rho=20, across all KK and all λint\lambda_{\mathrm{int}}. The indirect-effect correction is dead weight when non-stationarity is absent and becomes the load-bearing component of CAPO when it is present.

7 Related Work

Cooperative MARL credit assignment.

The opacity-learnability framing that motivates SeqAU originates with Wolpert and Tumer (2002). COMA (Foerster et al., 2018) operationalized the AU counterfactual through a centralized critic at O⁡(|𝒜|K)O(|\mathcal{A}|^{K}) marginalization cost. Closer in spirit, Dr.Reinforce (Castellini et al., 2025) combines policy gradients with aristocrat-utility difference rewards computed from the environment reward, but targets simultaneous-execution Dec-POMDPs and has no analog for the indirect effect that arises only under sequential execution. In the factored-policy limit, CAPO’s direct effect reduces to Dr.Reinforce’s aristocrat utility under additive rewards. Additive or factored team-reward decomposition in cooperative multi-agent RL dates back to Guestrin et al. (2002) and Kok and Vlassis (2006); the decomposed-critic family moves this principle from the reward to the value function, with DOP (Wang et al., 2021) assuming an additively factored QQ and VDN (Sunehag et al., 2018), QMIX (Rashid et al., 2018), FACMAC (Peng et al., 2021), and DAE (Li et al., 2022) using related value-side factorizations. All assume simultaneous decentralized execution in Dec-POMDPs, with no mechanism for one agent’s action to enter another agent’s input, so the indirect effect that characterizes the sequential setting is identically zero by construction. CAPO inherits this additive-reward decomposition principle but applies it to the reward rather than the value function, identifying per-agent components by closed-form regression rather than by gradient-based critic learning.

Sequential cooperative credit assignment.

The sequential prior work is comparatively sparse. HAPPO (Kuba et al., 2022) performs sequential per-agent updates with a cumulative importance-sampling prefix, paying the exponential-in-kk variance cost analyzed in Section 5; HA-GRPO is its critic-free GRPO variant. SeCA (Zang et al., 2023) imposes a virtual agent ordering and learns a counterfactual centralized QQ-critic conditional on the prefix of preceding agents’ actions, but the ordering is virtual (execution remains simultaneous and downstream agents do not actually condition on upstream actions), and the centralized QQ enumerates discrete actions, intractable for LLM token sequences. Seq-MADAC (Lu et al., 2025) uses a HAPPO-style sequential decomposition for hyperparameter configuration without a counterfactual baseline. Most relevant conceptually is Triantafyllou et al. (2025), who formalize the decomposition of the total counterfactual effect of an agent’s action in sequential multi-agent MDPs into an agent-specific effect (propagating through subsequent agents’ actions, analogous to CAPO’s indirect effect) and a state-specific effect (propagating through state transitions). Their estimator is a Shapley-value post-hoc attribution; CAPO turns the same direct-versus-indirect decomposition into a tractable policy-gradient estimator under the additive-reward assumption. Our work uses learnability maximization baseline which is in contrast with the optimal variance-reduction baseline (Kuba et al., 2021) for multi-agent settings.

Critic-free policy gradients for multi-agent LLMs.

A recent line adapts GRPO (DeepSeek-AI, 2025)’s critic-free within-group baseline to multi-agent LLM pipelines, with two families. Shared-baseline methods (MA-GRPO (Liu et al., 2025), AT-GRPO (Zhao et al., 2025), M-GRPO (Hong et al., 2025)) assign every agent the same trajectory or hierarchy-level advantage; HA-GRPO adds HAPPO’s cumulative importance-sampling prefix to correct sequential-update drift. Counterfactual methods estimate per-agent credit by intervening on upstream actions and observing downstream outputs. The two closest concurrent comparisons are C3 (Chen et al., 2026), which replays the downstream pipeline at alternative focal actions and reads actual environment rewards via a leave-one-out baseline (capturing the fixed-prefix counterfactual, but freezing downstream continuations to the rollout-collection distribution rather than the current joint policy, and paying one full reward evaluation per replay), and CCPO (Li et al., 2026b), which estimates counterfactual credit via topology-specific shortcuts (for example, “removing” the reasoner in a reasoner–solver pipeline by resampling the solver from the empty prompt); these shortcuts are tightly tied to the pipeline structure and do not extend to general sequential chains. Shapley-style alternatives such as SHARP (Li et al., 2026a) and Lazy Agents (Zhang et al., 2025) use multi-step causal attribution at correspondingly higher per-step cost; single-agent hindsight-credit work (Tan et al., 2026) is in the same wave but a different setting. CAPO’s distinguishing combination against this line is critic-free, reward-side (closed-form ridge regression rather than learned QQ or environment replay), uses current-policy fictitious continuations (rather than frozen-prefix replay), and is generic across sequential chains (no topology assumption beyond fixed execution order).

8 Conclusion

We have presented CAPO, a critic-free per-agent policy gradient for cooperative multi-agent teams under sequential execution. On the theoretical side, we extended the opacity-learnability framework of Wolpert and Tumer (2002) to the sequential setting and identified the unique learnability-maximizing prefix-conditional baseline, which subtracted from the team reward gives the Sequential Aristocrat Utility (SeqAU). On the algorithmic side, CAPO estimates the SeqAU advantage in closed form through an additive reward decomposition, an upstream-cancellation identity, and fictitious sampling for the indirect effect. The resulting estimator admits analytic bias and variance bounds, which we validate on a controlled sequential-bandit testbed.

Several directions remain open. The additivity assumption is exact when rewards separate across agents and gracefully lossy otherwise; heavily interaction-dependent rewards are a regime where a richer estimator may be preferable. Extension beyond one-step bandits to full sequential MDPs, and end-to-end evaluation on multi-LLM pipelines, are natural follow-ups.

Appendix A Sequential learnability: factoredness and optimality

This appendix gives the formal treatment deferred from Section 3. Appendix A.1 defines factoredness; Appendix A.2 shows that sequential difference utilities form a factored class; Appendix A.3 proves Theorem 1.

A.1 Factoredness

Definition 5 (Factoredness).

A per-agent utility gkg_{k} is factored with respect to the team reward RR if, for all ak1,ak2∈𝒜ka_{k}^{1},a_{k}^{2}\in\mathcal{A}_{k} and all prefixes a<ka_{<k},

sgn⁡[g¯k​(ak1,a<k)−g¯k​(ak2,a<k)]=sgn⁡[R¯k​(ak1,a<k)−R¯k​(ak2,a<k)],\mathrm{sgn}\!\bigl[\bar{g}_{k}(a_{k}^{1};a_{<k})-\bar{g}_{k}(a_{k}^{2};a_{<k})\bigr]\;=\;\mathrm{sgn}\!\bigl[\bar{R}_{k}(a_{k}^{1};a_{<k})-\bar{R}_{k}(a_{k}^{2};a_{<k})\bigr],

where U¯k(ak;a<k)=𝔼a>k∼π>k(⋅∣a≤k)[U(a)]\bar{U}_{k}(a_{k};a_{<k})=\mathbb{E}_{a_{>k}\sim\pi_{>k}(\cdot\mid a_{\leq k})}[U(a)] denotes the suffix-averaged form of any utility UU.

Factoredness aligns per-agent utility with team reward: every move that improves the suffix-averaged gkg_{k} at agent kk also improves the suffix-averaged team reward, and conversely. A utility satisfying factoredness is therefore a valid target for agent kk to optimize in place of RR.

A.2 Sequential difference utilities are factored

Proposition 6.

For any function D:∏j<k𝒜j→ℝD:\prod_{j<k}\mathcal{A}_{j}\to\mathbb{R}, the utility gk​(a)=R⁡(a)−D⁡(a<k)g_{k}(a)=R(a)-D(a_{<k}) satisfies the factoredness condition of Definition 5.

Proof.

The suffix-averaged form is g¯k​(ak,a<k)=R¯k​(ak,a<k)−D⁡(a<k)\bar{g}_{k}(a_{k};a_{<k})=\bar{R}_{k}(a_{k};a_{<k})-D(a_{<k}). Since D⁡(a<k)D(a_{<k}) does not depend on aka_{k}, it cancels in the difference g¯k​(ak1,a<k)−g¯k​(ak2,a<k)=R¯k​(ak1,a<k)−R¯k​(ak2,a<k)\bar{g}_{k}(a_{k}^{1};a_{<k})-\bar{g}_{k}(a_{k}^{2};a_{<k})=\bar{R}_{k}(a_{k}^{1};a_{<k})-\bar{R}_{k}(a_{k}^{2};a_{<k}), and the signs coincide. ∎∎

Proposition 6 justifies restricting the SeqAU search to sequential difference utilities: every such utility is a valid optimization target, so the question Theorem 1 answers is which baseline DD within this class maximizes learnability.

A.3 Proof of Theorem 1

We substitute the utility gk​(a)=R⁡(a)−D⁡(a<k)g_{k}(a)=R(a)-D(a_{<k}) into the sequential learnability expression (1) and minimize the denominator while showing the numerator is independent of DD.

Numerator.

For any aka_{k},

g¯k(ak;a<k)=𝔼a>k∼π>k(⋅∣a≤k)[R(a)−D(a<k)]=R¯k(ak;a<k)−D(a<k).\bar{g}_{k}(a_{k};a_{<k})\;=\;\mathbb{E}_{a_{>k}\sim\pi_{>k}(\cdot\mid a_{\leq k})}\!\bigl[R(a)-D(a_{<k})\bigr]\;=\;\bar{R}_{k}(a_{k};a_{<k})-D(a_{<k}).

Since D⁡(a<k)D(a_{<k}) does not depend on aka_{k}, it cancels in the difference g¯k​(ak1,a<k)−g¯k​(ak2,a<k)=R¯k​(ak1,a<k)−R¯k​(ak2,a<k)\bar{g}_{k}(a_{k}^{1};a_{<k})-\bar{g}_{k}(a_{k}^{2};a_{<k})=\bar{R}_{k}(a_{k}^{1};a_{<k})-\bar{R}_{k}(a_{k}^{2};a_{<k}), and the numerator of (1) is independent of DD.

Denominator.

By the law of total variance, conditioning on a<ka_{<k},

Var(a<k,a>k)|ak​[gk]=Vara<k​[g¯k​(ak,a<k)]+𝔼a<k​[Varπ>k|a≤k​[gk]].\mathrm{Var}_{(a_{<k},a_{>k})\mid a_{k}}[g_{k}]\;=\;\mathrm{Var}_{a_{<k}}\!\bigl[\bar{g}_{k}(a_{k};a_{<k})\bigr]\;+\;\mathbb{E}_{a_{<k}}\!\bigl[\mathrm{Var}_{\pi_{>k}\mid a_{\leq k}}[g_{k}]\bigr].

The inner variance in the second term is taken over a>ka_{>k} for fixed a≤ka_{\leq k}. Since D⁡(a<k)D(a_{<k}) is constant under this conditioning, the second term equals 𝔼a<k​[Varπ>k|a≤k​[R]]\mathbb{E}_{a_{<k}}[\mathrm{Var}_{\pi_{>k}\mid a_{\leq k}}[R]] and does not depend on DD. Maximizing learnability therefore reduces to minimizing the first term, Vara<k​[R¯k​(ak,a<k)−D⁡(a<k)]\mathrm{Var}_{a_{<k}}[\bar{R}_{k}(a_{k};a_{<k})-D(a_{<k})], which is invariant to adding an aka_{k}-independent constant to DD.

Taking the joint expectation 𝔼a<k,ak∼ρ(⋅∣a<k)\mathbb{E}_{a_{<k},\,a_{k}\sim\rho(\cdot\mid a_{<k})} in the denominator of the learnability expression and applying Var⁡[Y]=𝔼⁡[Y2]−(𝔼⁡[Y])2\mathrm{Var}[Y]=\mathbb{E}[Y^{2}]-(\mathbb{E}[Y])^{2}, the minimization reduces to the quadratic loss

minD𝔼a<k𝔼ak∼ρ(⋅∣a<k)[(R¯k(ak;a<k)−D(a<k))2].\min_{D}\;\mathbb{E}_{a_{<k}}\mathbb{E}_{a_{k}\sim\rho(\cdot\mid a_{<k})}\!\bigl[(\bar{R}_{k}(a_{k};a_{<k})-D(a_{<k}))^{2}\bigr].

Pointwise in a<ka_{<k}, the minimizer of this loss is the conditional expectation of R¯k​(ak,a<k)\bar{R}_{k}(a_{k};a_{<k}) under ρ(⋅∣a<k)\rho(\cdot\mid a_{<k}),

D∗(a<k)=𝔼ak∼ρ(⋅∣a<k)[R¯k(ak;a<k)]=𝔼ak′∼ρ(⋅∣a<k),a>k′∼π>k(⋅∣a<k,ak′)[R(ak′,a<k,a>k′)],D^{*}(a_{<k})\;=\;\mathbb{E}_{a_{k}\sim\rho(\cdot\mid a_{<k})}\!\bigl[\bar{R}_{k}(a_{k};a_{<k})\bigr]\;=\;\mathbb{E}_{a_{k}^{\prime}\sim\rho(\cdot\mid a_{<k}),\;a_{>k}^{\prime}\sim\pi_{>k}(\cdot\mid a_{<k},a_{k}^{\prime})}\!\bigl[R(a_{k}^{\prime},a_{<k},a_{>k}^{\prime})\bigr],

which is independent of the choice of (ak1,ak2)(a_{k}^{1},a_{k}^{2}) and therefore maximizes Λkseq\Lambda_{k}^{\mathrm{seq}} at every prefix and every move pair simultaneously. This completes the proof. ∎

Appendix B Derivation of the upstream-cancellation identity

We derive the direct/indirect decomposition of the CAPO advantage stated in Eq. (6). Substitute the additive model f^​(a)=∑j=1Kφ^j​(aj)\hat{f}(a)=\sum_{j=1}^{K}\hat{\varphi}_{j}(a_{j}) into the SeqAU counterfactual advantage AkLS​(a≤k)=QkLS​(a≤k)−VkLS​(a<k)A_{k}^{\mathrm{LS}}(a_{\leq k})=Q_{k}^{\mathrm{LS}}(a_{\leq k})-V_{k}^{\mathrm{LS}}(a_{<k}) of (3). Expanding QkQ_{k} under additivity and splitting the sum over jj into upstream (j<kj<k), focal (j=kj=k), and downstream (j>kj>k):

QkLS​(a≤k)\displaystyle Q_{k}^{\mathrm{LS}}(a_{\leq k}) =𝔼π(k−1)​[∑j=1Kφ^j​(aj)|a≤k]\displaystyle\;=\;\mathbb{E}_{\pi^{(k-1)}}\!\Bigl[\textstyle\sum_{j=1}^{K}\hat{\varphi}_{j}(a_{j})\;\Big|\;a_{\leq k}\Bigr]
=∑j<kφ^j​(aj)⏟upstream+φ^k​(ak)+∑j>k𝔼π(k−1)​[φ^j​(aj)∣a≤k],\displaystyle\;=\;\underbrace{\sum_{j<k}\hat{\varphi}_{j}(a_{j})}_{\text{upstream}}\;+\;\hat{\varphi}_{k}(a_{k})\;+\;\sum_{j>k}\mathbb{E}_{\pi^{(k-1)}}\!\bigl[\hat{\varphi}_{j}(a_{j})\mid a_{\leq k}\bigr], (10)

where the upstream terms exit the expectation because each φ^j\hat{\varphi}_{j} with j<kj<k is a function of aja_{j} alone (under additivity) and therefore a deterministic function of the prefix a<ka_{<k} that QkQ_{k} already conditions on. Similarly expanding VkV_{k}:

VkLS​(a<k)\displaystyle V_{k}^{\mathrm{LS}}(a_{<k}) =𝔼π(k−1)​[∑j=1Kφ^j​(aj)|a<k]\displaystyle\;=\;\mathbb{E}_{\pi^{(k-1)}}\!\Bigl[\textstyle\sum_{j=1}^{K}\hat{\varphi}_{j}(a_{j})\;\Big|\;a_{<k}\Bigr]
=∑j<kφ^j​(aj)⏟same upstream+𝔼π(k−1)​[φ^k​(ak)∣a<k]+∑j>k𝔼π(k−1)​[φ^j​(aj)∣a<k].\displaystyle\;=\;\underbrace{\sum_{j<k}\hat{\varphi}_{j}(a_{j})}_{\text{same upstream}}\;+\;\mathbb{E}_{\pi^{(k-1)}}\!\bigl[\hat{\varphi}_{k}(a_{k})\mid a_{<k}\bigr]\;+\;\sum_{j>k}\mathbb{E}_{\pi^{(k-1)}}\!\bigl[\hat{\varphi}_{j}(a_{j})\mid a_{<k}\bigr]. (11)

The upstream sum ∑j<kφ^j​(aj)\sum_{j<k}\hat{\varphi}_{j}(a_{j}) is identical in Eqs. (10) and (11): both conditional expectations are taken under the same joint policy π(k−1)\pi^{(k-1)} and both condition on the same prefix a<ka_{<k}; the upstream terms depend only on a<ka_{<k} and are therefore deterministic constants under both conditionings. Subtracting (11) from (10), the upstream contributions cancel identically, yielding

AkLS​(a≤k)=φ^k​(ak)−𝔼π(k−1)​[φ^k​(ak)∣a<k]⏟DkA_{k}^{\mathrm{LS}}(a_{\leq k})\;=\;\underbrace{\hat{\varphi}_{k}(a_{k})\;-\;\mathbb{E}_{\pi^{(k-1)}}[\hat{\varphi}_{k}(a_{k})\mid a_{<k}]}_{D_{k}}
+∑j>k(𝔼π(k−1)​[φ^j​(aj)∣a≤k]−𝔼π(k−1)​[φ^j​(aj)∣a<k])⏟Ik.\;+\;\underbrace{\sum_{j>k}\!\Bigl(\mathbb{E}_{\pi^{(k-1)}}[\hat{\varphi}_{j}(a_{j})\mid a_{\leq k}]\;-\;\mathbb{E}_{\pi^{(k-1)}}[\hat{\varphi}_{j}(a_{j})\mid a_{<k}]\Bigr)}_{I_{k}}.

The conditional expectation in DkD_{k} is taken over aka_{k} alone (since φ^k\hat{\varphi}_{k} depends only on aka_{k}), and under the autoregressive factorization of π(k−1)\pi^{(k-1)} this is the marginal expectation 𝔼ak′∼πk(⋅∣a<k)[φ^k(ak′)]\mathbb{E}_{a_{k}^{\prime}\sim\pi_{k}(\cdot\mid a_{<k})}[\hat{\varphi}_{k}(a_{k}^{\prime})], giving the form of Eq. (6). ∎

Appendix C Proofs of the theoretical properties (Section 5)

This appendix collects the proofs of Theorems 2, 3, and 4.

C.1 Proof of Theorem 2 (general bias bound)

Let Q^k​(a≤k)=𝔼π(k−1)​[f^∣a≤k]\hat{Q}_{k}(a_{\leq k})=\mathbb{E}_{\pi^{(k-1)}}[\hat{f}\mid a_{\leq k}] and V^k​(a<k)=𝔼π(k−1)​[f^∣a<k]\hat{V}_{k}(a_{<k})=\mathbb{E}_{\pi^{(k-1)}}[\hat{f}\mid a_{<k}], and let Qk,VkQ_{k},V_{k} denote the corresponding quantities for the true conditional mean ff. By definition, A^kLS=Q^k−V^k\hat{A}_{k}^{\mathrm{LS}}=\hat{Q}_{k}-\hat{V}_{k} and Ak=Qk−VkA_{k}=Q_{k}-V_{k}, so

Δk​(a≤k)=(Q^k​(a≤k)−Qk​(a≤k))−(V^k​(a<k)−Vk​(a<k)).\Delta_{k}(a_{\leq k})\;=\;\bigl(\hat{Q}_{k}(a_{\leq k})-Q_{k}(a_{\leq k})\bigr)\;-\;\bigl(\hat{V}_{k}(a_{<k})-V_{k}(a_{<k})\bigr).

Using linearity of expectation and f^−f=ε\hat{f}-f=\varepsilon,

Q^k​(a≤k)−Qk​(a≤k)=𝔼π>k|a≤k​[ε⁡(a)],V^k​(a<k)−Vk​(a<k)=𝔼π≥k|a<k​[ε⁡(a)].\hat{Q}_{k}(a_{\leq k})-Q_{k}(a_{\leq k})\;=\;\mathbb{E}_{\pi_{>k}\mid a_{\leq k}}\!\bigl[\varepsilon(a)\bigr],\qquad\hat{V}_{k}(a_{<k})-V_{k}(a_{<k})\;=\;\mathbb{E}_{\pi_{\geq k}\mid a_{<k}}\!\bigl[\varepsilon(a)\bigr].

Expanding the VkV_{k}-residual by conditioning on aka_{k},

𝔼π≥k|a<k​[ε]=𝔼ak∼πk​[𝔼π>k|a≤k​[ε]],\mathbb{E}_{\pi_{\geq k}\mid a_{<k}}[\varepsilon]\;=\;\mathbb{E}_{a_{k}\sim\pi_{k}}\!\bigl[\mathbb{E}_{\pi_{>k}\mid a_{\leq k}}[\varepsilon]\bigr],

so

Δk(a≤k)=𝔼π>k|a≤k[ε]−𝔼ak′∼πk,a>k′∼π>k(⋅∣a<k,ak′)[ε].\Delta_{k}(a_{\leq k})\;=\;\mathbb{E}_{\pi_{>k}\mid a_{\leq k}}[\varepsilon]\;-\;\mathbb{E}_{a_{k}^{\prime}\sim\pi_{k},\,a_{>k}^{\prime}\sim\pi_{>k}(\cdot\mid a_{<k},a_{k}^{\prime})}[\varepsilon].

Write this as a difference of conditional expectations of a single random quantity, ε⁡(a)\varepsilon(a), under two different distributions over (ak,a>k)(a_{k},a_{>k}): one fixes aka_{k} at its observed value and averages a>ka_{>k} under π>k(⋅∣a≤k)\pi_{>k}(\cdot\mid a_{\leq k}); the other averages aka_{k} under πk(⋅∣a<k)\pi_{k}(\cdot\mid a_{<k}) and, conditional on aka_{k}, a>ka_{>k} under π>k(⋅∣a<k,ak)\pi_{>k}(\cdot\mid a_{<k},a_{k}). Decomposing by the tower property,

Δk​(a≤k)=𝔼ak′∼πk​[𝔼π>k|a≤k​[ε⁡(a<k,ak,a>k)]−𝔼π>k|a<k,ak′​[ε⁡(a<k,ak′,a>k′)]].\Delta_{k}(a_{\leq k})\;=\;\mathbb{E}_{a_{k}^{\prime}\sim\pi_{k}}\!\left[\mathbb{E}_{\pi_{>k}\mid a_{\leq k}}[\varepsilon(a_{<k},a_{k},a_{>k})]-\mathbb{E}_{\pi_{>k}\mid a_{<k},a_{k}^{\prime}}[\varepsilon(a_{<k},a_{k}^{\prime},a_{>k}^{\prime})]\right].

Adding and subtracting 𝔼π>k|a<k,ak′​[ε⁡(a<k,ak,a>k)]\mathbb{E}_{\pi_{>k}\mid a_{<k},a_{k}^{\prime}}[\varepsilon(a_{<k},a_{k},a_{>k})] inside the bracket splits the integrand into two channels. The first channel,

𝔼π>k|a≤k​[ε⁡(a<k,ak,a>k)]−𝔼π>k|a<k,ak′​[ε⁡(a<k,ak,a>k)],\mathbb{E}_{\pi_{>k}\mid a_{\leq k}}[\varepsilon(a_{<k},a_{k},a_{>k})]-\mathbb{E}_{\pi_{>k}\mid a_{<k},a_{k}^{\prime}}[\varepsilon(a_{<k},a_{k},a_{>k})],

captures how the downstream-conditioning distribution changes with the focal action; it is bounded by ∥ε∥∞⋅∥π>k(⋅∣a<k,ak)−π>k(⋅∣a<k,ak′)∥1\|\varepsilon\|_{\infty}\cdot\|\pi_{>k}(\cdot\mid a_{<k},a_{k})-\pi_{>k}(\cdot\mid a_{<k},a_{k}^{\prime})\|_{1}. The second channel,

𝔼π>k|a<k,ak′​[ε⁡(a<k,ak,a>k)−ε⁡(a<k,ak′,a>k)],\mathbb{E}_{\pi_{>k}\mid a_{<k},a_{k}^{\prime}}[\varepsilon(a_{<k},a_{k},a_{>k})-\varepsilon(a_{<k},a_{k}^{\prime},a_{>k})],

captures the sensitivity of the residual to the focal action; it is bounded in absolute value by δkε​(a−k)=maxak,ak′⁡|ε⁡(a<k,ak,a>k)−ε⁡(a<k,ak′,a>k)|\delta_{k}^{\varepsilon}(a_{-k})=\max_{a_{k},a_{k}^{\prime}}|\varepsilon(a_{<k},a_{k},a_{>k})-\varepsilon(a_{<k},a_{k}^{\prime},a_{>k})|. Taking absolute values and the πk\pi_{k} expectation,

|Δk(a≤k)|≤𝔼π≥k|a<k[δkε(a−k)]+∥ε∥∞⋅maxak,ak′∥π>k(⋅∣a<k,ak)−π>k(⋅∣a<k,ak′)∥1,|\Delta_{k}(a_{\leq k})|\;\leq\;\mathbb{E}_{\pi_{\geq k}\mid a_{<k}}[\delta_{k}^{\varepsilon}(a_{-k})]\;+\;\|\varepsilon\|_{\infty}\cdot\max_{a_{k},a_{k}^{\prime}}\|\pi_{>k}(\cdot\mid a_{<k},a_{k})-\pi_{>k}(\cdot\mid a_{<k},a_{k}^{\prime})\|_{1},

which is the statement of Theorem 2. ∎

C.2 Specialization under factored policies

Under a factored joint policy π⁡(a)=∏kπk​(ak)\pi(a)=\prod_{k}\pi_{k}(a_{k}), the downstream conditional distribution is independent of the focal action: π>k(⋅∣a<k,ak)=π>k(⋅∣a<k)=∏j>kπj(⋅)\pi_{>k}(\cdot\mid a_{<k},a_{k})=\pi_{>k}(\cdot\mid a_{<k})=\prod_{j>k}\pi_{j}(\cdot). Hence the second channel of the bound in Theorem 2 vanishes identically. From the first channel, using the factored structure,

𝔼π≥k|a<k​[δkε​(a−k)]=𝔼aj∼πj,j≠k​[δkε​(a−k)].\mathbb{E}_{\pi_{\geq k}\mid a_{<k}}[\delta_{k}^{\varepsilon}(a_{-k})]\;=\;\mathbb{E}_{a_{j}\sim\pi_{j},\,j\neq k}\!\bigl[\delta_{k}^{\varepsilon}(a_{-k})\bigr].

The residual ε​(a)=f^​(a)−f​(a)\varepsilon(a)=\hat{f}(a)-f(a) is computed from φ^\hat{\varphi} fit on μ\mu-rollouts, and the advantage we want is under π\pi-rollouts. When μj≠πj\mu_{j}\neq\pi_{j}, the ridge-fit f^\hat{f} differs between the two measures only through the Gram matrix; under factored rollouts the mismatch propagates as

|𝔼π−k​[ε⁡(a<k,ak,a>k)]−𝔼μ−k​[ε⁡(a<k,ak,a>k)]|≤‖ε‖∞⋅∑j≠k‖πj−μj‖1.\bigl|\mathbb{E}_{\pi_{-k}}[\varepsilon(a_{<k},a_{k},a_{>k})]-\mathbb{E}_{\mu_{-k}}[\varepsilon(a_{<k},a_{k},a_{>k})]\bigr|\;\leq\;\|\varepsilon\|_{\infty}\cdot\sum_{j\neq k}\|\pi_{j}-\mu_{j}\|_{1}.

This is the standard bound for changing measures under a bounded integrand. Substituting and applying the triangle inequality,

|Δk​(ak)|≤ 2​‖ε‖∞⋅∑j≠k‖πj−μj‖1≤ 2​(K−1)​δ¯​‖ε‖∞,|\Delta_{k}(a_{k})|\;\leq\;2\|\varepsilon\|_{\infty}\cdot\sum_{j\neq k}\|\pi_{j}-\mu_{j}\|_{1}\;\leq\;2(K-1)\bar{\delta}\|\varepsilon\|_{\infty},

using δ¯=maxj⁡‖πj−μj‖1\bar{\delta}=\max_{j}\|\pi_{j}-\mu_{j}\|_{1}, which is the specialization claimed in the second half of Theorem 2. ∎

C.3 Proof of Theorem 3 (advantage variance)

Under the additive reward f⁡(a)=∑kφk∗​(ak)f(a)=\sum_{k}\varphi_{k}^{*}(a_{k}), the ridge-regression solution can be written as

φ^=(λ​I+Ψ⊤​Ψ)−1​Ψ⊤​r.\hat{\varphi}\;=\;(\lambda I+\Psi^{\top}\Psi)^{-1}\Psi^{\top}r.

We work at the population level, replacing the sample Gram matrix Ψ⊤​Ψ\Psi^{\top}\Psi by N​GμNG_{\mu}; the fluctuations of Ψ⊤​Ψ\Psi^{\top}\Psi around N​GμNG_{\mu} contribute an O⁡(1/N)O(1/\sqrt{N}) correction that does not affect the KK-scaling statement.

At the population level, write r=Ψ​φ∗+ηr=\Psi\varphi^{*}+\eta where η∈ℝN\eta\in\mathbb{R}^{N} has i.i.d. entries with 𝔼⁡[ηi∣Ψ]=0\mathbb{E}[\eta_{i}\mid\Psi]=0 and Var⁡(ηi)≤Rmax2\mathrm{Var}(\eta_{i})\leq R_{\max}^{2} (the additive assumption makes Ψ​φ∗\Psi\varphi^{*} the exact conditional mean). Then

φ^−φ∗=(λ​I+N​Gμ)−1​(Ψ⊤​η−λ​φ∗),\hat{\varphi}-\varphi^{*}\;=\;(\lambda I+NG_{\mu})^{-1}\bigl(\Psi^{\top}\eta-\lambda\varphi^{*}\bigr),

and the ridge bias term vanishes in the full-coverage regime relative to the variance. For the variance contribution,

Cov⁡(φ^)⪯(λ​I+N​Gμ)−1​𝔼​[Ψ⊤​η​η⊤​Ψ]​(λ​I+N​Gμ)−1⪯Rmax2λ+N​κμ​I,\mathrm{Cov}(\hat{\varphi})\;\preceq\;(\lambda I+NG_{\mu})^{-1}\,\mathbb{E}[\Psi^{\top}\eta\eta^{\top}\Psi]\,(\lambda I+NG_{\mu})^{-1}\;\preceq\;\frac{R_{\max}^{2}}{\lambda+N\kappa_{\mu}}\,I,

where we used 𝔼⁡[Ψ⊤​η​η⊤​Ψ]⪯Rmax2⋅Ψ⊤​Ψ\mathbb{E}[\Psi^{\top}\eta\eta^{\top}\Psi]\preceq R_{\max}^{2}\cdot\Psi^{\top}\Psi (by the variance bound on η\eta) and (λ​I+N​Gμ)−1⪯(λ+N​κμ)−1​I(\lambda I+NG_{\mu})^{-1}\preceq(\lambda+N\kappa_{\mu})^{-1}I.

The direct-effect component Dk(a≤k)=φ^k(ak)−𝔼πk(⋅∣a<k)[φ^k]D_{k}(a_{\leq k})=\hat{\varphi}_{k}(a_{k})-\mathbb{E}_{\pi_{k}(\cdot\mid a_{<k})}[\hat{\varphi}_{k}] is a linear functional wD⊤​φ^w_{D}^{\top}\hat{\varphi} whose coefficient vector wDw_{D} has one indicator entry of weight 11 for φ^k​(ak)\hat{\varphi}_{k}(a_{k}) and a probability vector of ℓ2\ell_{2} norm at most 11 on the marginal expectation, so ‖wD‖22≤2\|w_{D}\|_{2}^{2}\leq 2. Hence

Var⁡(Dk​(a≤k))=wD⊤​Cov​(φ^)​wD≤‖wD‖22⋅Rmax2λ+N​κμ≤2​Rmax2λ+N​κμ,\mathrm{Var}\!\bigl(D_{k}(a_{\leq k})\bigr)\;=\;w_{D}^{\top}\mathrm{Cov}(\hat{\varphi})w_{D}\;\leq\;\|w_{D}\|_{2}^{2}\cdot\frac{R_{\max}^{2}}{\lambda+N\kappa_{\mu}}\;\leq\;\frac{2R_{\max}^{2}}{\lambda+N\kappa_{\mu}},

independent of KK. For the full advantage A^kLS=Dk+Ik\hat{A}_{k}^{\mathrm{LS}}=D_{k}+I_{k} under exact indirect-effect evaluation, the indirect effect adds further coordinates to the linear functional. For each j>kj>k, the coefficient on φ^j​(aj)\hat{\varphi}_{j}(a_{j}) is Pπ>k​(aj∣a≤k)−Pπ>k​(aj∣a<k)P_{\pi_{>k}}(a_{j}\mid a_{\leq k})-P_{\pi_{>k}}(a_{j}\mid a_{<k}), whose squared sum over aja_{j} is bounded by ∥P(⋅∣a≤k)−P(⋅∣a<k)∥1⋅∥P(⋅∣a≤k)−P(⋅∣a<k)∥∞≤2\|P(\cdot\mid a_{\leq k})-P(\cdot\mid a_{<k})\|_{1}\cdot\|P(\cdot\mid a_{\leq k})-P(\cdot\mid a_{<k})\|_{\infty}\leq 2. Summing over j>kj>k contributes at most 2​(K−k)2(K-k) to ‖w‖22\|w\|_{2}^{2}, giving the worst-case bound Var⁡(A^kLS)≤(2+2​(K−k))​Rmax2/(λ+N​κμ)\mathrm{Var}(\hat{A}_{k}^{\mathrm{LS}})\leq(2+2(K-k))R_{\max}^{2}/(\lambda+N\kappa_{\mu}). In the factored-policy limit, the indirect-effect coefficients all vanish and the KK-independent direct-effect bound applies to the full advantage. ∎

C.4 Proof of Theorem 4 (gradient MSE)

Let gk∗=𝔼π(k−1)​[Ak​sk]g_{k}^{*}=\mathbb{E}_{\pi^{(k-1)}}[A_{k}\,s_{k}] be the true gradient and g^k=1L​∑ℓA^kLS,(ℓ)​sk(ℓ)\hat{g}_{k}=\frac{1}{L}\sum_{\ell}\hat{A}_{k}^{\mathrm{LS},(\ell)}s_{k}^{(\ell)} the CAPO estimator. Decompose

g^k−gk∗=1L​∑ℓ(Ak​sk)(ℓ)−gk∗⏟Evar+1L​∑ℓΔk(ℓ)​sk(ℓ)⏟Ebias.\hat{g}_{k}-g_{k}^{*}\;=\;\underbrace{\frac{1}{L}\sum_{\ell}(A_{k}s_{k})^{(\ell)}-g_{k}^{*}}_{E_{\text{var}}}\;+\;\underbrace{\frac{1}{L}\sum_{\ell}\Delta_{k}^{(\ell)}s_{k}^{(\ell)}}_{E_{\text{bias}}}.

The first term is the standard REINFORCE estimation error of a bounded random variable and has

𝔼​‖Evar‖2≤1L​Varπ(k−1)​(Ak​sk).\mathbb{E}\|E_{\text{var}}\|^{2}\;\leq\;\frac{1}{L}\mathrm{Var}_{\pi^{(k-1)}}(A_{k}s_{k}).

The second term is a sum of LL i.i.d. bounded quantities; its second moment is

𝔼​‖Ebias‖2≤𝔼π(k−1)​[Δk2​‖sk‖2]≤Bk2⋅𝔼π(k−1)​[‖sk‖2],\mathbb{E}\|E_{\text{bias}}\|^{2}\;\leq\;\mathbb{E}_{\pi^{(k-1)}}[\Delta_{k}^{2}\|s_{k}\|^{2}]\;\leq\;B_{k}^{2}\cdot\mathbb{E}_{\pi^{(k-1)}}[\|s_{k}\|^{2}],

using |Δk|≤Bk|\Delta_{k}|\leq B_{k}. Applying (a+b)2≤2​a2+2​b2(a+b)^{2}\leq 2a^{2}+2b^{2} to g^k−gk∗=Evar+Ebias\hat{g}_{k}-g_{k}^{*}=E_{\text{var}}+E_{\text{bias}},

𝔼​‖g^k−gk∗‖2≤2L​Varπ(k−1)​(Ak​sk)+ 2​Bk2⋅𝔼π(k−1)​[‖sk‖2],\mathbb{E}\|\hat{g}_{k}-g_{k}^{*}\|^{2}\;\leq\;\frac{2}{L}\mathrm{Var}_{\pi^{(k-1)}}(A_{k}s_{k})\;+\;2B_{k}^{2}\cdot\mathbb{E}_{\pi^{(k-1)}}[\|s_{k}\|^{2}],

which is the bound of Theorem 4. Crucially, the fictitious rollouts are drawn from π(k−1)\pi^{(k-1)} directly rather than reweighted from μ\mu, so no cumulative importance-sampling prefix enters either term. ∎

Appendix D Per-agent advantage MSE at K=16K=16

Figure 4 breaks the K=16K=16 result of Section 6.1 down by agent index. CAPO’s MSE is essentially flat across agents, consistent with the KK- and position-independence of Theorem 3. HA-GRPO grows with agent index as the cumulative importance-sampling prefix accumulates noise at downstream agents. MA-GRPO is flat at a high level (shared-baseline variance does not depend on position). C3 is comparable to CAPO on average but with markedly higher variance across agent positions due to prefix-filtering effective-sample-size loss.

Appendix E Non-stationarity parametrization in the optimization experiment

The non-stationarity parameter ρ\rho used in Section 6.3 controls how strongly each agent’s conditional policy depends on its upstream action, which in turn determines the severity of the distribution shift over downstream behavior when an upstream agent’s policy is updated. Concretely, the initial joint policy is drawn as follows. For each agent k≥1k\geq 1 and each upstream-action value c∈𝒜k−1c\in\mathcal{A}_{k-1}, we first sample a base conditional distribution πkbase(⋅∣c)∼Dirichlet(𝟏)\pi^{\mathrm{base}}_{k}(\cdot\mid c)\sim\mathrm{Dirichlet}(\mathbf{1}) over 𝒜k\mathcal{A}_{k}, and then concentrate it toward the diagonal by the exponential tilt

πk(a∣c)∝πkbase(a∣c)⋅exp(ρ⋅𝟏[a=c]).\pi_{k}(a\mid c)\;\propto\;\pi^{\mathrm{base}}_{k}(a\mid c)\cdot\exp\bigl(\rho\cdot\mathbf{1}[a=c]\bigr). (12)

At ρ=0\rho=0 the tilt is trivial and πk(⋅∣c)=πkbase(⋅∣c)\pi_{k}(\cdot\mid c)=\pi^{\mathrm{base}}_{k}(\cdot\mid c), which is approximately uniform. As ρ\rho grows, mass concentrates on the action a=ca=c, so agent kk’s behavior becomes increasingly dictated by agent k−1k-1’s action. This does not change what optima the team reward admits—φk\varphi_{k} and gk​ℓg_{k\ell} are drawn independently of ρ\rho—but it determines how much the distribution over downstream behavior shifts when an upstream agent’s policy is updated during training. Agent 0, which has no upstream conditioning variable, is drawn uniformly from the simplex regardless of ρ\rho. Across the three values ρ∈{0,1,2}\rho\in\{0,1,2\} that we sweep in Section 6.3, and the four values ρ∈{0,5,10,20}\rho\in\{0,5,10,20\} swept in the direct-effect ablation of Section 6.4, the diagonal mass of the initial conditional policies increases from near 1/|𝒜|1/|\mathcal{A}| (near-uniform) to near 11 (near-deterministic), spanning the range from mild to severe sequential-update non-stationarity.

Appendix F Per-cell AUC and regret trajectories for the optimization experiment

Figure 5 shows the full per-cell AUC breakdown corresponding to Table 1 in Section 6.3: normalized regret AUC as a function of λint\lambda_{\mathrm{int}} for each (K,ρ)(K,\rho) combination. Figure 6 shows the raw per-iteration regret trajectories for the same sweep. Both views are consistent with the summary table: MA-GRPO is competitive with CAPO at small KK, CAPO pulls ahead for K≥6K\geq 6, and HA-GRPO degrades rapidly with KK.

Appendix G Regret trajectories for the direct-effect ablation

Figures 7–11 show regret as a function of cumulative real environment calls for CAPO versus CAPO-Direct, one figure per value of the interaction strength λint∈{0,0.25,0.5,0.75,1.0}\lambda_{\mathrm{int}}\in\{0,0.25,0.5,0.75,1.0\}. Each figure is a K×ρK\times\rho grid with rows K∈{2,4,8}K\in\{2,4,8\} and columns ρ∈{0,5,10,20}\rho\in\{0,5,10,20\}; curves average over 300 seeds with shaded standard errors. The qualitative picture matches the AUC summary of Figure 3: CAPO-Direct is at least as good at ρ=0\rho=0, and CAPO pulls ahead cleanly as ρ\rho grows.

Appendix H Hyperparameters and experimental protocol

Table 2 collects the hyperparameter values used in each experiment. Across all experiments, agents have action sets of size A=4A=4, the policy-gradient step size is η=0.3\eta=0.3, team rewards have observation noise σ=0.5\sigma=0.5, and per-agent ground-truth advantages are computed by exact marginalization. The CAPO implementation differs by experiment as noted: the MSE diagnostics of Sections 6.1–6.2 use the closed-form ridge solver of (5), so the experiments test Theorem 3 directly; the optimization experiments of Sections 6.3–6.4 use per-agent fictitious-sample averaging (CAPO-Direct’s φ^\hat{\varphi} component is the closed-form ridge solver). The optimization comparisons match real-environment interactions across methods: each method’s outer-iteration count TmT_{m} is set so that Tm×(per-iteration real-env cost)T_{m}\times(\text{per-iteration real-env cost}) is constant across methods, anchored to Tc3=25T_{\mathrm{c3}}=25 for the CAPO-vs-baselines comparison (Section 6.3) and to CAPO-Direct with Tanchor=25T_{\mathrm{anchor}}=25 for the ablation (Section 6.4). C3’s O⁡(K2)O(K^{2}) per-iteration replay cost therefore reduces its effective TT relative to MA-GRPO, HA-GRPO, and CAPO. The paper-faithful CAPO evaluates f^\hat{f} (a table lookup of the ridge-fit φ^\hat{\varphi}) on fictitious continuations; these cost only policy forward passes and no real-environment evaluations.
